reference.source: Clinical genetics and connective tissue disorder references
clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive subtype caused by biallelic ADAMTS2 mutations, which abolish procollagen I N-proteinase and prevent cleavage of the N-terminal propeptide of type I procollagen.
Hallmark is extreme skin fragility with soft, doughy, redundant and sagging skin giving an aged appearance, together with severe, easy bruising.
The skin is fragile and lax rather than markedly hyperextensible with atrophic scarring — a useful contrast with classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Characteristic facies include puffy oedematous eyelids, epicanthic folds and micrognathia, with blue sclerae and often delayed closure of the fontanelles.
Umbilical and inguinal herniae, rectal prolapse, short stature and osteopenia are frequent.
Electron microscopy of skin shows irregular, ribbon-like collagen fibrils with 'hieroglyphic' cross-sections — highly suggestive.
The name derives from a homologous, well-described disorder of cattle and sheep ('dermatosparaxis', meaning torn skin).
Coagulation studies are typically normal despite dramatic bruising, and surgical wounds heal poorly, so unnecessary operations should be avoided.
reference.pathophysiology: Dermatosparaxis Ehlers-Danlos syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in ADAMTS2, which encodes procollagen I N-proteinase, a secreted metalloproteinase that removes the amino-terminal propeptide from type I (and, less critically, types II and III) procollagen during collagen maturation. When this propeptide is not excised, partially processed pN-collagen is incorporated into fibrils and sterically interferes with normal lateral packing, producing the irregular, ribbon-like fibrils seen on electron microscopy. Because type I collagen provides tensile strength to skin, fascia, blood vessels and other tissues, the poorly assembled matrix is profoundly fragile and lax, explaining the sagging redundant skin, easy tearing and bruising, herniae and organ prolapse. The disorder is the enzymatic counterpart of arthrochalasia Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, in which the same processing step fails because the collagen substrate itself lacks the cleavage site rather than because the enzyme is deficient.
additionalDifferentials: Cutis laxa syndromes (elastin, fibulin or ATP7A related)
Geroderma osteodysplasticum and De Barsy syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Electron microscopy of a skin biopsy for ribbon-like ('hieroglyphic') collagen fibrils
Biochemical collagen studies demonstrating accumulation of unprocessed pN-collagen
Coagulation screen (characteristically normal) to exclude a bleeding diathesis
Clinical and imaging assessment of herniae and pelvic-floor or rectal prolapse
redFlags: Extensive spontaneous bruising or large haematomata
Skin lacerations or wound dehiscence after minor trauma or surgery
Incarceration or strangulation of a hernia
Signs of visceral or bladder rupture
reference.prognosis: Skin and tissue fragility persist lifelong and cause considerable morbidity from bruising, wounds, herniae and prolapse; with careful, conservative management life expectancy is often near normal, though severe neonatal presentations occur.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the sagging skin as a cutis laxa syndrome
Attributing severe bruising to a primary bleeding disorder or to non-accidental injury
Proceeding to elective surgery in tissues that tear and heal poorly
Overlooking herniae, prolapse or bladder complications
